AMD delivers record quarter as Data Center segment revenue grows 97% year-over-year, driven by record sales of AMD Instinct GPUs and AMD EPYC CPUs
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov. 03, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) today announced financial results for the third quarter of 2026. Third quarter revenue was $13.4 billion, gross margin was 54%, operating income was $2.8 billion, net income was $2.4 billion and diluted earnings per share was $1.46. On a non-GAAP
(*)
basis, gross margin was 56%, operating income was $3.9 billion, net income was $3.5 billion and diluted earnings per share was $2.09.
“We delivered a record quarter with revenue exceeding the high end of our guidance as Data Center segment sales nearly doubled year-over-year,” said Dr. Lisa Su, AMD chair and CEO. “Demand for our Instinct and EPYC products continued to strengthen, and we expect growth to accelerate further in the fourth quarter as we scale Helios and ‘Venice’ production. With our leadership product portfolio and deep customer and supply chain relationships, we are confident in our ability to sustain very strong revenue growth and expanding profitability over the coming years.”
“Third quarter revenue grew 45% year-over-year to a record $13.4 billion, while non-GAAP earnings per share grew 74%, demonstrating the significant operating leverage in our business model as our Data Center business drives scale,” said Jean Hu, AMD executive vice president, chief financial officer and treasurer. “Our fourth-quarter outlook reflects accelerating revenue and earnings growth, driven by strong demand across our Data Center portfolio.”

Gaming business revenue was $773 million, down 40% year-over-year, due to lower semi-custom and graphics revenue.
Embedded segment revenue was $1.1 billion, up 29% year-over-year, led by growth in aerospace and defense, automotive, communications and industrial end markets.

Our mission
We build the foundation for understanding AI’s economic impact. The Anthropic Economic Index tracks how AI tools are being used around the world and across every sector of the economy. Alongside regular Economic Index reports, we produce novel research that studies the economic implications of AI, and fund ambitious external research.
Producing reliable data to guide policy
The speed of AI development means the stakes are unusually high. We need reliable data to inform the decisions that workers, employers, and policymakers make about the future. Our research provides evidence to address uncertainty and help society navigate this transition.

We’re highlighting 20 scientific foundations, institutions, and research groups from around the world that we’ve partnered with in an expansion of our
AI for Science program
, which gives free Claude credits to researchers working on high-impact scientific projects.
We started the AI for Science program in May 2025 with the belief that AI could significantly speed up scientific progress. Our goal is to increase access to AI tools and resources to enable researchers to deepen and expand their own scientific work. (Over the last few months, we’ve also launched our discounted
Team plan for scientists
and have supported hundreds of projects across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, climate science, and mathematics.)
Scientists have told us that they’re working with Claude to generate hypotheses, design experiments, swiftly analyze complex data, and communicate findings. With scientists at the center of this transformation, the field is setting the questions and developing the research projects that will help us tackle some of humanity’s toughest problems.
Over the past year, we’ve started to expand this work and partner with scientific organizations to build collaborative research projects. For instance, we partnered with
HHMI Janelia Research Campus
to develop the
Model Hardware Standard
(MHS), a shared specification that lets AI agents safely operate lab instruments. MHS is currently in research preview. We also support the
Allen Institute
, a leader in creating large open datasets and tools to advance research on the brain, cells, and the immune system. The institute is building teams of AI agents to analyze that data, turning months of manual analysis into hours.
AI for Science began by supporting individual scientists. By partnering with institutions and foundations, we’re now able to reach more researchers across many fields. Many of these projects will also produce public goods that benefit the wider scientific community: open datasets, open-source software, open standards, and shared libraries. We look forward to seeing how AI resources can expand what scientists can attempt and lead to new discoveries.
Science funders and societies
Science funders and societies play an enormous role in finding and funding original, high-impact projects. We’re sharing Claude credits with the following organizations, which will distribute these resources to ambitious researchers aiming to use AI for scientific research:
The Alfred P. Sloan Foundation.
Founded in 1934, it supports original research and education in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and economics.
The Simons Foundation.
This foundation advances the frontiers of research in mathematics and basic sciences through grants and its Flatiron Institute.
Schmidt Sciences.
Founded in 2024 by Eric and Wendy Schmidt, it works to accelerate scientific knowledge and breakthroughs with the most promising, advanced tools to support a thriving planet. The organization prioritizes research in areas poised for impact, including AI and advanced computing, astrophysics, biosciences, climate, and space—and supports researchers in a variety of disciplines through its science systems program.
Open Source for Science Fund, a program of Renaissance Philanthropy.
This is a time-bound philanthropic fund at Renaissance Philanthropy sustaining and evolving the open-source software stack that underpins science.
The US National Science Foundation.
This $9 billion federal agency established by Congress in 1950 promotes the progress of science, advances national health and defense, and funds competitive research and education, accounting for about 25% of federal support for basic research at US colleges and universities.
CAS, a division of the American Chemical Society.
For more than a century, CAS has indexed the world’s published chemistry, and it maintains the CAS REGISTRY®, the standard system for identifying chemical substances.
Institutions
Leading research institutions produce some of the world’s most important scientific advances, data, instruments, and tools. These institutional partners will use Claude credits inside their organizations to enable scientific discovery:
Space Telescope Science Institute.
STScI runs science operations for NASA’s Hubble, James Webb, and Roman space telescopes. Managed by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA), STScI also holds one of the largest astronomy data archives used by scientists worldwide.
Wellcome Sanger Institute.
One of the world’s leading genomics centers, it generates genomic and functional data at scale, with work that spans human genetics, biodiversity, and drug development.
The Francis Crick Institute.
Based in London, it’s one of Europe’s largest biomedical research institutes, with more than 100 research groups studying the biology behind health and disease.
Imperial College London, Department of Life Sciences.
One of Europe’s largest life science departments, it conducts research ranging from the structure of single molecules to whole ecosystems, with a focus on health, disease, and climate resilience.
EMBL.
The European Molecular Biology Laboratory is Europe’s intergovernmental life science laboratory, with six sites across the continent delivering both research and services across experimental and computational approaches in biology. EMBL’s European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) hosts a number of key open data resources that biologists use every day, such as Ensembl, Protein Data Bank in Europe, and Europe PMC.
Gladstone Institutes.
An independent biomedical research institute in San Francisco, it integrates AI and data science across its work on cardiology, neurology, infectious diseases, cancer, and autoimmune diseases.
Research projects and initiatives
As part of this work, we’re also continuing to support innovative research by providing Claude credits directly to specific research initiatives, focusing on problems with the potential for large public impact. The new projects are:
FlyWire, Princeton University (neuroscience).
It produced the first complete wiring map of an adult fruit fly’s brain and develops open data and tools for connectomics, enabling researchers to discover how neural circuits give rise to perception and behavior.
LEAP, Columbia University (Earth system).
Learning the Earth with Artificial Intelligence and Physics is a National Science Foundation center that combines machine learning with physics to improve how climate models capture clouds, oceans, and land.
AstroPath, Johns Hopkins University (cancer research).
Built by a pathologist and an astrophysicist from the Mark Foundation Center for Advanced Genomics and Imaging and the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, AstroPath uses calibration methods from astronomical surveys to image tumors cell by cell, with measurements consistent across slides and labs.
gnomAD, Broad Institute (genomics and rare disease).
The Genome Aggregation Database pools DNA data from over 800,000 people into an open reference of human genetic variation that researchers and clinical labs around the world use to support rare disease discovery and diagnosis.
Tau Ceti (mathematics).
This open, community-driven project is building a shared autoformalized library of mathematics in Lean, a language that lets computers check every proof.
Centre for Population Genomics.
A joint initiative between Australia’s Garvan Institute of Medical Research and Murdoch Children’s Research Institute, it increases the inclusion of Australia’s multicultural communities in genomic resources and builds tools for rare disease diagnosis.
What’s next
Many of these collaborations are still in their early stages, and we’re eager to see how they can support novel research and scientific discovery. We look forward to sharing the impact of this work and showcasing new ways of working in these scientific fields.
As AI changes how science is done, our AI for Science program will continue to support and collaborate with scientists, institutions, and foundations. We hope to expand these efforts to even more partners around the world.

Today, we’re inviting members of the life sciences community to apply to work with us on special projects. We’re looking for proposals from principal investigators and their research groups at academic institutions, nonprofits, or government labs who want to use Claude to investigate key questions in causal human biology, structural and computational molecular biology, medicinal chemistry, drug discovery, and clinical science.
You can submit a
proposal for a project here
.
Over 8–12 weeks, guest investigators will work directly with Anthropic researchers on a problem of interest and produce the analyses, artifacts, and tools that will be most helpful for them in their work. Our team will run our models and harnesses at no cost to them.
We’ll work together to publish these outputs and open-source the accompanying data and code. Guest investigators retain the rights to their data at every step during their project. They will also have the rights to any independent follow-on research that might come out of our collaboration.
We’re looking for applicants who can clearly explain how they would benefit from direct collaboration with Anthropic’s researchers. Applicants should also make a reasonable case that their outputs (e.g., preliminary discoveries, answers to open questions, open-source datasets, or public resources) can be produced within the 8- to 12-week collaboration period. There may be an option for extension beyond the initial collaboration period for some projects.
We understand that the results for most open problems of interest will take much longer to validate, but we’re looking for proposals that can produce some preliminary evidence in a relatively short amount of time.
We aren’t asking for guest investigators to give us their data, either in the application or during the collaboration, and we’re requesting that applicants include only publicly available information in their application materials.
Applications will be open for approximately 14 days, and we’ll strive to notify selected participants by email approximately 14 days after applications close. We look forward to potentially expanding this effort in the future as we learn more about how we can best support the scientific community.
This program is one of several initiatives Anthropic is pursuing to invest more heavily in the life sciences and the broader scientific research community. Scientists who would like direct access to our most capable publicly available models for biology can apply to join our
Life Sciences Verification Program
. We’ve also continued to support researchers through our
AI for Science initiative
, which provides scientists with Claude credits to accelerate their progress toward making scientific discoveries.

Monthly API credits for Max, Ultra, and Team plans
Updated over a week ago
Copy for LLM
Max, Ultra, and Team plans include monthly credits for the Claude Platform. Use them to build Claude into your own apps and agents with the Claude API. This article explains who's eligible, how to claim your credit, what it covers, and what happens when it runs out.
Available on Max, Ultra, and Team plans, including discounted Team plans. Free, Pro, and Enterprise plans aren't eligible.
Monthly credits by plan
Plan
Monthly credit
Max
$100
Ultra
$200
Team (Standard seats)
$20 per seat*
Team (Premium seats)
$100 per seat*
Discounted Team plans (Nonprofit, Scientists)
$20 USD per Standard seat and $100 USD per Premium seat*
*On Team plans, credits for all seats are pooled into one monthly balance, capped at $500. For example, a team with three Standard seats and two Premium seats receives $260 a month. The pool is calculated from the seats on the plan when the credits are granted.
Eligibility
Active plan.
Your Max, Ultra, or Team subscription must be active and in good standing.
Seven days on the plan.
New subscribers can claim once they've been on an eligible plan for seven days.
Mobile subscriptions.
You can subscribe on the web, iOS, or Android. Claim your credits on claude.ai in a web browser.
No payment method needed.
You don't need to add a card on Claude Platform to claim or use the credit.
How to claim your credit
To claim your credit, you link a Claude Console organization to your plan. Credits go to that organization each month.
Before you begin, you need:
On your Claude plan:
Max or Ultra:
to be the subscriber
Team:
to be a Primary Owner or Owner
In the Console organization:
the Owner, Admin, or Billing role. If you don't have a Console organization yet, you can create one during the claim flow or at
platform.claude.com
.
To claim your credit:
On claude.ai, go to
Settings > Billing
as a Max or Ultra subscriber, or
Organization settings > Billing
as a Team Owner or Primary Owner.
In the
API credits
section, select "Link organization."
Choose the Console organization you want to receive the credits, or create a new one.
Review the
Supplemental Credit Terms
, then Link organization.
Your credits appear in that organization's balance, ready to use.
Important:
You can link only one Console organization, and each Console organization can receive credits from only one plan. You can't change the linked organization yourself, so choose the one you plan to build in. To change it later,
contact support
.
Tip:
Sign in to the Claude Console with the same email you use on claude.ai. If you’re seeing errors during the linking flow, please try again in a few hours.
What the credits cover
The credits work with any available Claude model on the Claude Platform, including:
The Claude API (Messages API and Message Batches API)
The Playground in the Claude Console
Claude Managed Agents
The Claude Agent SDK
The credits don’t apply to:
Interactive Claude Code in the terminal, IDE, desktop, or web
Extra usage in Claude, Claude Code, or Claude Cowork
Claude on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, or Microsoft Foundry
How the credits work
Refreshes each billing cycle.
New credits arrive shortly after your plan payment goes through. On annual plans, credits arrive monthly.
Doesn't roll over.
Unused credits expire at the end of each billing cycle.
Used first.
Your monthly credits are spent before any credits you've purchased.
Shared across the organization.
Everyone with an API key in the linked organization draws from the same balance.
Separate from your plan limits.
The credits don’t change your usage limits in Claude, Claude Code, or Claude Cowork.
Visible in the Console.
All credits appear on the
Billing
page (platform.claude.com/settings/billing) in the Claude Console with their amount and expiry date.
What happens when your credits run out
If the organization has purchased credits or auto-reload,
usage continues and draws from those.
If the organization has no other credits,
API requests stop until your next monthly credits arrive. Usage is never charged to your Claude plan. To keep going, buy credits or turn on auto-reload in the Console.
If your organization is invoiced through Anthropic sales,
usage beyond the credits is billed as usual.
If your plan changes
Cancel, downgrade to an ineligible plan, or refund.
New credits stop. Credits you already have stay usable until they expire.
Upgrade from Max to Ultra.
You receive prorated credits right away, then $200 each billing cycle after that.
Move from Max or Ultra to Team.
Your Max or Ultra link ends. A Team Owner or Primary Owner can claim the team's credits once the Team plan has been active for seven days.
For Team Owners and Primary Owners
One claim for the whole team.
One owner links a Console organization and claims the pooled credit, up to $500 a month.
The pool follows your seat count.
It's calculated from the seats on your plan each time credits are deposited. For example, a team with three Standard seats and two Premium seats receives $260 a month. Adding another Premium seat would increase the next cycle’s credits to $360.
Control who spends it.
Everyone with an API key in the linked organization can use the balance. To limit usage by project or teammate, set
workspace spend limits
in the Console.
Frequently asked questions
Why can't I use the credits for Claude Code?
The credits are for building your own apps and agents on the Claude Platform. They don't cover interactive Claude Code sessions or extra usage after you hit your plan's limits.
Why don't I see the offer yet?
We’re rolling out API credits over a few days so we might not have gotten to you yet. The offer appears after you've been on an eligible plan for seven days. If you're past seven days and still don't see it, check that you're on a Max, Ultra, or Team plan and that you have one of the required roles. If you think you should be eligible but don’t see the API credits,
contact support
.
Is this the same as the Agent SDK credits announced in June?
No. That credit isn't available. API credits cover the Claude API, Claude Managed Agents, and the Claude Agent SDK, and you claim it into a Console organization.
Can I split my credits across multiple organizations?
No. Credits go to a single Console organization.
I'm on a Pro plan. Can I get this credit?
No. The credits are available on Max, Ultra, and Team plans only.
Does this cover
claude -p
?
API credits cover
claude -p
and the Claude Agent SDK when you run them yourself with an API key from your linked Claude Console organization, because that usage is billed as Agent SDK usage. When you're signed in with your Claude plan instead,
claude -p
and Agent SDK usage still draw from your plan's usage limits and don't use your API credits. Runs started by the Claude Code GitHub Action, an IDE extension or the Claude desktop app count as Claude Code usage, so API credits don't cover them, even with
-p
.

AI-Generated Summary
FLUX 3 Image Klein Base
and its distilled variant combine Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct for text conditioning, a diffusion transformer, and an autoencoder to generate and edit images at high resolution.
TensorRT LLM VisualGen accelerates inference on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with NVFP4 quantization, fused PrimsTS GEMM kernels, and torch.compile, delivering up to 1.62x faster text-to-image and 1.58x faster image-to-image generation over BF16 on a single B200.
Quantized attention options include cuDNN FP8 and VC-Attention FP8; VC-Attention FP8 with a repair budget of 0.005 achieved 1.18x speedups for both Base and distilled models at 2048x2048 with LPIPS scores of 0.086 and 0.151.
Sol-Attention sparse attention with τ=1.0 and 12 initial dense steps provided 1.30x faster denoising plus decoding for Base, while 16 dense steps prioritized fidelity at 1.24x.
Cache-DiT step caching nearly halved Base latency at both 1024x1024 and 2048x2048, reaching 1.94x speedup at the higher resolution with an LPIPS of 0.033.
Multi-GPU scaling with CFG and Ulysses parallelism on eight B200 GPUs reduced median T2I latency from 14.90 to 3.00 seconds for Base and from 2.73 to 1.08 seconds for distilled, with denoising speedups of 6.01x and 4.44x.
Next Steps

to understand the optimization APIs.

to engage with the development team.

Learn more
When deploying diffusion models in design tools, image editors, and visual production workflows, developers must account for inference latency. Generating an image requires multiple sequential passes through a model with billions of parameters, and higher resolutions increase attention costs.
FLUX 3 Image Klein is an image editing and generation model from Black Forest Labs (BFL) trained on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 and optimized for NVIDIA GPUs. It offers
Base
and
distilled
checkpoints for different latency and fidelity requirements.
This tutorial shows how to configure FLUX 3 Image Klein in NVIDIA TensorRT LLM VisualGen to take advantage of fused kernels, multi-GPU parallelism, FP8/NVFP4 support, caching, and attention optimizations. It compares latency and changes in generated outputs across optimizations. In the reported 2048×2048 tests on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU, combined optimizations delivered up to 3.46x faster text-to-image (T2I) and 4.45x faster image-to-image (I2I) generation for FLUX 3 Image Klein Base compared with uncompiled BF16 inference. The tutorial includes deployment instructions and YAML configurations for applying these optimizations to your workloads.
FLUX 3 inference with TensorRT LLM VisualGen
FLUX 3 Image Klein combines Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct for text conditioning, a diffusion transformer (DiT) to refine image latents, and an autoencoder to decode latents into images and encode I2I reference inputs. Klein processes text, noisy target-image, and optional reference-image streams independently before combining them through joint attention.
TensorRT LLM VisualGen, a dedicated runtime within TensorRT LLM, supported BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 variants at launch. On an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU, NVFP4 delivered up to 1.62x faster T2I and 1.58x faster I2I generation than BF16. Figure 2 compares generation latency, while Figure 1 compares example outputs. The following sections use NVFP4 as the starting point for further optimization.

TensorRT LLM VisualGen accelerates NVFP4 DiT inference with optimized general matrix multiplication (GEMM) kernels and epilogue fusion, low-precision and sparse attention, caching, and multi-GPU execution. Unless otherwise noted, the following benchmarks use
torch.compile
and seed 0. Base uses 50 denoising steps and a CFG scale of 3.5; the distilled Klein uses 16 denoising steps.

VisualGen supports BFL’s prequantized NVFP4 DiT checkpoints for
FLUX 3 Image Klein
and
FLUX 3 Image Klein Base

GEMM kernel optimization
TensorRT LLM VisualGen uses FlashInfer’s PrimsTS FP8/NVFP4 GEMM kernels, built with CUTLASS
Primitives
and
Task Scheduling
to accelerate quantized inference. Tuned for FLUX 3 tensor shapes and enabled by default, they combine optimized GEMMs with fused epilogues, including GEMM with SwiGLU and query, key, and value (QKV) projections with query/key normalization and rotary position embeddings (RoPE). See
FlashInfer PR #5758
for more details.
At launch, the pinned NVFP4 PrimsTS kernels delivered 1.02–1.10x faster T2I generation on B200 than the autotuned TensorRT LLM NVFP4 GEMM implementation.

Quantized and sparse attention
Attention is a major bottleneck in high-resolution image generation. In the reported 2048×2048 NVFP4 T2I tests on B200, VANILLA BF16 attention accounted for approximately 60% of DiT GPU kernel time for both Base and distilled Klein. VisualGen supports two approaches to reducing this cost: quantized attention with

VC-Attention paper
.
Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) measures perceptual differences between generated images. In the following comparisons, lower scores indicate greater similarity to the corresponding VANILLA baseline output.
Compared with VANILLA BF16 attention, cuDNN FP8 delivered generation speedups of 1.08x for Base and 1.09x for the 16-step distilled Klein. The corresponding LPIPS scores were 0.072 and 0.161. Cache-DiT reduces FLUX 3 Image Klein inference latency by reusing intermediate transformer outputs across denoising steps without retraining or modifying model weights. The VisualGen runtime in TensorRT LLM scales FLUX 3 Image Klein using classifier-free guidance (CFG) and Ulysses sequence parallelism. Base assigns positive/negative branches to separate GPU groups and partitions each branch’s sequence with Ulysses; distilled runs without CFG and uses Ulysses alone.

Accelerating Reinforcement Learning Weight Refit with the Reshard Collective

By
Youngeun Kwon
,
Kaushik Kandadi Suresh
,

,

and

AI-Generated Summary
Refit transfers updated model weights from training GPUs to inference GPUs during reinforcement learning post-training, and its communication payload grows with model size to an estimated 10 TB per refit for today's largest open weight models.
The Reshard collective reformulates refit as a DTensor-to-DTensor transfer, moving only the theoretical minimum data between arbitrary source and destination layouts instead of using a gather-and-broadcast approach.
NCCL M2N Reshard
implements this collective by deriving exact shard intersections and grouping NVLink domain replicas to eliminate redundant network transfers.
In NeMo RL benchmarks on NVIDIA DGX H100 and DGX GB200 systems, Reshard refit achieved a 2.7x to 5.7x speedup over conventional gather-and-broadcast refit across models including Qwen 3 235B and DeepSeek v3 671B.
A hybrid approach in NeMo RL applies Reshard to feed-forward projection weights that dominate the payload while retaining gather-and-broadcast for smaller weights to maintain functional coverage.
Next Steps
Read the
NeMo RL refit guide
to understand supported backends, layouts, and precision modes.
Review the
NCCL Reshard configuration requirements
for implementation details.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
During
reinforcement learning (RL)
post-training, training trajectories are generated on the fly by running inference with the current policy model. For training efficiency, it is common to run inference and training in parallel on separate GPU resources in a disaggregated setup. Although the policy model is updated only on the training GPUs, the system must periodically refresh the weights on the inference GPUs with the latest parameters generated on the training GPUs. This transfer of model weights between training and inference GPUs is called
refit
.
Refit involves two defining characteristics that pose challenges. First, inference and training have different computational requirements, so the weights are distributed differently across inference and training instances by having different parallel mappings (data, context, tensor, expert, and pipeline parallelism).
Second, because refit must update all model weights on the inference GPUs, the communication payload is on the order of the total size of the model’s weights. This payload is already very large for the latest frontier models and is expected to continue growing. Together, these characteristics mean that refit requires high-performance communication across a wide variety of distributed source and destination layouts.
This post explains how AI training frameworks can address these refit challenges using the Reshard collective, a new type of collective communication primarily designed to accelerate RL weight refit. NCCL M2N Reshard, an open source reference implementation of the Reshard collective, is available through the
NVIDIA/nccl-extensions
GitHub repo.
Challenges of current weight refit methods as models scale
Existing refit implementations commonly use a
gather-and-broadcast approach
to handle differences between training and inference layouts.
The typical gather-and-broadcast weight refit sequence for every model parameter is structured as follows:
Training GPUs all-gather their local shards to reconstruct the complete parameter.
The complete parameter tensor is broadcast to the inference GPUs.
Each inference GPU retains the shard required by its local layout.
Using the complete tensor as an intermediate representation makes it straightforward to transfer weights between different layouts. However, an inference GPU receives the full parameter even when it needs only a shard. This process creates redundant communication in both the gathering and broadcasting phases, which is suboptimal.
The size of this communication grows with the model size, which continues to scale. For example,
Kimi K3 contains 2.8 trillion parameters
, while
Qwen 3.8 2.4T A95B contains 2.4 trillion
parameters. Assuming BF16 weights at two bytes per parameter, their weight sizes are approximately 5.6 TB and 4.8 TB, respectively.
Accounting for both the all-gather and broadcast stages gives an estimated logical payload of approximately twice the size of the model’s weights (Table 1).
Model
Size in bytes
Refit payload estimate (all-gather+broadcast)
Kimi K3
5.6 TB
≈11.2 TB
Qwen 3.8 2.4T A95B
4.8 TB
≈9.6 TB
Table 1. Two-stage logical payload estimate assuming BF16 weights
For today’s largest open weight models, the communication payload already reaches around 10 TB per refit, which must be performed at every training step. As LLMs continue to scale, the overhead associated with this large payload will become even more significant. As a result, a more sophisticated approach is needed to perform weight refit that reduces the actual payload size while properly accounting for diverse weight layouts.
Reformulating refit as a DTensor-to-DTensor transfer problem
To overcome these limitations, start from the principle that refit should transfer only the theoretical minimum amount of weight data. However, achieving this presents several challenges. Training and inference instances can use different parallelism configurations and GPU counts, producing different shard boundaries. A destination shard may therefore need to be assembled from portions of several source shards, and vice versa.
Replication further complicates the mapping since the same weights may be available from multiple source GPUs or required by multiple destination GPUs. It is nontrivial to determine which source GPUs should send which tensor regions to each destination while achieving high performance across all possible configurations.
The key to addressing this challenge is to identify the right abstraction for this unique communication pattern. The team turned to the existing PyTorch
distributed tensor (DTensor)
abstraction, which is designed to represent tensors that are sharded or replicated across GPUs under different forms of data and model parallelism. The key insight is that weight refit can be reformulated as resharding a DTensor from the training layout to the inference layout, regardless of the parallelism configurations used by the two instances.
A DTensor layout is described by the tensor’s global shape, a
device mesh
specifying the logical arrangement of GPUs, and
placements
specifying how the tensor is sharded or replicated across that mesh. Refit can use the source description to specify where the updated weights reside and the destination description to specify which weights each inference GPU needs.
For example, consider an 8 x 8 weight matrix split by rows across two training GPUs and by columns across four inference GPUs. Assuming the tensor is sharded in the row dimension on the training GPUs and sharded in the column dimension on the inference GPUs, each training GPU holds a 4 x 8 shard, while each inference GPU needs an 8 x 2 shard. Each destination can obtain its required shard by receiving a 4 x 2 region from each source. These regions follow directly from the overlap between the source and destination shards, as illustrated in Figure 1.
Figure 1. Direct shard-to-shard transfer of an 8 x 8 tensor from two training GPUs to four inference GPUs. The pattern can be cleanly abstracted as a DTensor-to-DTensor reshard
As the figure shows, any kind of sharded tensor can be easily represented as a DTensor format, and the refit can be redefined as a DTensor-to-DTensor reshard problem. This finding provides the foundation for the Reshard collective.
Reshard collective communication for DTensor-to-DTensor transfers
Reshard is a new type of collective communication call for arbitrary DTensor-to-DTensor transfers. Like all-reduce, reduce-scatter, all-gather, broadcast, and so on, reshard defines a communication pattern that applications can invoke as one operation. It transfers the values of a logical tensor from its source distribution into its destination distribution.
A Reshard call can be specified simply by the source and destination DTensor descriptions. This abstraction not only simplifies the refit problem, but also encapsulates the communication logic in a library, allowing the underlying algorithms to evolve and improve independently of the application.
NCCL M2N Reshard
is open source, provided to the community as the first reference implementation of the Reshard collective. Built on NCCL, this implementation transfers a tensor distributed across M source GPUs into the layout required by N destination GPUs. In RL refit, the training GPUs form the source group and the inference GPUs form the destination group.
Figure 2 shows how this implementation accepts the layout descriptions and local buffers to carry out the Reshard operation.
Figure 2. The nccl.m2n.reshard example that transfers a tensor sharded across four training GPUs (TP4) into replicas on four inference GPUs (DP4)
How NCCL M2N Reshard unlocks maximum network bandwidth
NCCL M2N Reshard first derives the exact intersections between source and destination shards, then maps those transfers onto the physical GPU network topology. Instead of sending every source contribution independently to every destination replica, NCCL M2N groups replicas by
NVIDIA NVLink
domain. Within each domain, it distributes the incoming contributions as evenly as possible across the replica ranks, so each receiving rank receives a distinct subset of the total data over the network.
The receiving ranks then exchange those subsets over NVLink, enabling every replica to assemble the complete shard without duplicating network traffic. If replicas span multiple NVLink domains, one copy of each contribution is forwarded through the domains, and the same balanced local exchange occurs within each domain. Network transfer and NVLink replication are pipelined to hide each other’s latency.
Figure 3 illustrates this data movement scheme for a tensor moving from TP4 on the source to TP2 x DP2 on the destination, with all four destination GPUs in one NVLink domain. With direct point-to-point transfers (Figure 3a), each source shard is sent to both data parallel (DP) replicas. As a result, each shard is transferred twice over the network redundantly. This means that each shard gets roughly half the network bandwidth (assuming each shard saturates the network bandwidth).
NCCL M2N Reshard transfers each source shard across the network just once, supplying each destination GPU with half of its required data (Figure 3b). The destination GPUs exchange the missing half over NVLink. For example, destination GPU 0 receives S0 from source GPU 0 over the network and S1 from destination GPU 2 over NVLink. Network transfers and NVLink exchanges proceed concurrently. This way, each shard gets the full network bandwidth.
Figure 3. Naive Direct P2P sends each source shard across the two DP replicas (left). With NCCL M2N Reshard, each destination GPU receives part of its data directly from the source over the network and the rest from another destination GPU over NVLink (right)
Demonstrating the Reshard collective with NVIDIA NeMo RL
To demonstrate the effectiveness of the Reshard collective for weight refit, a reference implementation is provided in the
NVIDIA NeMo RL
framework. NeMo RL is an open source framework designed to streamline and scale RL post-training. The clear abstraction of the Reshard collective makes the required implementation within the framework relatively simple. For a given parallelism configuration, the framework only needs to provide a DTensor description for each parameter for training and inference instances, which should be straightforward because DTensor was designed for this purpose.
In practice, however, the variety of layer types and the diversity in how training and inference engines shard parameters under each parallelism configuration make it challenging to handle every edge case through the Reshard collective.
To develop an efficient and sustainable design, we built on the key observation that feed-forward projection weights in the transformer block dominate the weight refit payload. In the latest LLMs, these weights account for around 95% of the model’s parameters.
Based on this observation, our design uses a hybrid approach in which dominant feed-forward projection weights take the reshard path, while all other small weights (for example, QKV projection or mamba weights) use the conventional gather-and-broadcast refit path, which is optimized for broad functional coverage. This approach combines efficient reshard communication for most of the payload with the same functional coverage as conventional gather-and-broadcast refit.
The sharding layout can change at runtime as nodes are added or removed during failure recovery. To accommodate changes in GPU membership, frameworks can either destroy and recreate the communication group or use
NCCL shrink and grow APIs
to adjust the existing communicator group. NeMo RL currently uses the first approach for resiliency support. Resiliency support using NCCL shrink and grow APIs is planned for future updates.
RL weight refit performance benchmark results
Table 2 summarizes reshard-based refit latencies measured using the
NeMo RL implementation
introduced above. The benchmarks cover a range of models on NVIDIA DGX H100 (NVL8) and NVIDIA DGX GB200 (NVL72) systems. Across various benchmarks, the reshard refit achieves a speedup of 2.7x to 5.7x over conventional gather-and-broadcast refit.

This new refit is designed for trillion-parameter models. In our refit-only microbenchmark, Reshard refit took only 4.3 seconds for the Qwen3.8 2.4T BF16 model, demonstrating its effectiveness at the trillion-parameter scale for which it was designed.
Get started with reshard weight refit using NeMo RL
The reference implementation in the NVIDIA NeMo RL framework enables you to adopt and extend this approach for your own RL workloads.
To enable the reshard refit path in NeMo RL, use the following configuration:

generation:
colocated:
enabled: false

NeMo RL refit guide
and

describe the supported backends, layouts, and precision modes for this feature.

items.title: Agent Distraction Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, w
items.content:
Agent Distraction
- Google Developers Blog
Agent Distraction
NOV. 6, 2026
Sam Saccone
Senior Staff Software Engineer
Madhuri Garikapati
Senior Staff Data Scientist
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
What is easy for humans to skim past in code, agents see as a call to action. They do not know better, latching on to that which is littered across the files read during the planning and research phase of the coding journey.
As agents' agency through tools and skills grows the ability for side-quests scales proportionally. Obsolete specs, long resolved bugs, and lagging documentation no longer rest in long forgotten corners of the codebase, but rather are unintentionally ingested as context indirecting and misdirecting the next wave of coders - the agents. This indirection is not free: in the best case it only costs tokens, steps, and time - in the worst case it distracts and grounds the agent on falsehoods leading to incorrect logic and decisions during implementation.
Measuring how often agents fall into these traps across millions of monthly sessions is impossible with manual human review - we need an objective signal derivable from the code itself. Inline TODO(bug/...) comments provide the perfect proxy. TODOs tend to be left behind long after the underlying bug is resolved or abandoned, while the linked bug ticket acts as the canonical record. By cross-referencing every TODO an agent encounters against the TODO's bug status and the user's prompt, we can automatically separate valid work from wasted detours at scale.
The Cost
By leveraging the distributed traces of agent interactions across thousands of engineers and over hundreds of millions of individual agent steps, we quantify the impact of TODO distractions in the codebase and how agents act on them:
Nearly 1 in 7 sessions are exposed (13%):
Of the millions of file-reading sessions, 13% of sessions exposed the agent to inline TODO(bug/...) or FIXME(bug/...) bug references.
6% trigger secondary action—and 83% of those are unprompted:
While agents ignored the comment in 94% of encounters, in 6% the agent took subsequent action targeting that bug ID. Over 4 in 5 of those actions (83% sessions) were completely unprompted—the developer didn’t ask for the bug.
41% chase closed dead ends, 57% trigger scope creep:
Cross-referencing the unprompted detours against live bug status exposes two distinct failure modes:
Over two-fifths of unprompted detours chased tickets that were already closed—split between already fixed/verified bugs (32%) and obsolete/won't-fix dead ends (9%), with an additional 2% hitting duplicate or restricted tickets.
In over half of unprompted detours, the bug was still open (NEW/ASSIGNED/ACCEPTED), and the agent expanded its work (61% lookup only; 39% edited code) to investigate or modify an issue the developer never asked to touch.
Controlling for developer, codebase complexity, task type, model tier, number of files read, initial prompt length, and the step where the bug reference appeared, using a multi-way fixed-effects regression with developer-clustered standard errors, we see that unprompted bug detours add substantial overhead (all stat sig p<0.0001). Per session:
70% more steps
77% more tokens
105% more wait time
How this plays out
The Obsolete Detour:
In the following trajectory we can observe how this drift plays out. During an investigation into an unrelated bug The agent views SurfaceControlTest.java and sees // TODO(bug/XXX)
This bug, while fixed in 2023, remains lingering in the codebase leading to subsequent investigation distraction across Steps with the agent digging into the bug to learn more.
The Eager Agent:
In the trajectory the agent encountered a TODO in the bug it was investigating and decided (unprompted) to "fix" the code
The agent executed multiple Code Search and internal knowledge search queries for the bug ultimately resulting in the agent changing the ModelDownloaderV1 code. Later in the trajectory the human challenged the scope creep.
With the model when admitting it was an incorrect increase in scope:
While in both of these cases they were only trivial to minor detours - they were real distractions costing time, tokens, and human intervention.
What we did
As part of addressing this finding at scale we created agents that scrubbed the totality of our codebases, finding bug references in the code that were marked as fixed or obsolete for cleanup. That step alone however was not enough to determine if the TODOs in the codebase were load-bearing or not. The agents had to go further looking at the history of the bug, the file, and changes to the codebase, at times spanning years of history. Only in cases where the agent was able to confirm that the TODO and the intent behind the TODO was obsolete did our agent send a change for review to delete it from the codebase. As a result of this multi-layer approach, our todo cleaner has been able to remove thousands of actually obsolete references over the last 6 months exceeding 95% acceptance from human reviewers.
The weight of distraction.
In recap, as we task agents on more and more ambitious problems, "agent friendly codebases" require more than just the code in the hotpath being healthy. The forgotten corners of the codebase now more than ever carry a significant tax levied against agents.
Tooling like presubmit analyzers, entire corpus scanners, and automated coding agents to remediate dead-todos offer out of the box ready to scale solutions to address the tax enabling a healthier and distraction free codebase for agents to thrive.
Projects that once were on the backburner to cleanup lingering debt but deprioritized due to perceived low value need to be reevaluated with the new agents acting at scale on your codebase.

items.title: Cost per task: Using cheap classifiers to route across Gemini models and thinking levels Per-token API prices keep falling, yet engineering bills for autonomous coding agents keep
items.content:
Cost per task: Using cheap classifiers to route across Gemini models and thinking levels
- Google Developers Blog
Cost per task: Using cheap classifiers to route across Gemini models and thinking levels
NOV. 3, 2026
Sergio Villani
Technical Solutions
Google Cloud AI
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Per-token API prices keep falling, yet engineering bills for autonomous coding agents keep climbing. Price per million tokens isn't the metric that actually governs production economics anymore. The dominating metric is now cost per successful task: total spend across every loop iteration, tool call, retry and internal thinking pass divided by the number of tasks that pass verification.
When an agent calls a high-thinking reasoning configuration for every micro-decision in its harness, you're paying deep-reasoning prices for questions a lightweight configuration already answers accurately. To prevent this unnecessary overhead, consider adding a lightweight routing layer that can intercept routine decisions before they ever reach an expensive reasoning model.
That is the premise behind wiring TypeSafe's Jev classifier in front of Google Antigravity's model calls. Rather than generating text token by token, Jev—a specialized structured-output classifier designed for high-throughput decision pipelines—evaluates structured classification primitives in a single forward pass: a Choice from a list, a numeric Score or a Noul, which returns a 0 to 1 probability for a binary statement.
For full disclosure, Google has no partnership with TypeSafe, and this article is not an endorsement of TypeSafe or its products. Jev is used here as one example of a lightweight classifier, and the same routing pattern can be built with other classifiers, including Google-native ones. The
Getting started with discriminative models
codelab, for example, runs the same kind of classifier on DiffusionGemma, Google DeepMind's open-weights model, in your own Google Cloud project.
We ran a 50-question, auto-graded, coding-agent benchmark against live Gemini and Jev APIs to test whether a near-free classifier can route each task to the cheapest model that still gets it right. Here's what we learned:
1. Regex and token-length harness routers collapse on unseen agent tasks
The naive way to ask Jev to route a coding task is a single broad Choice question:
simple
or
complex
. When we tested that first on 16 coding-agent tasks, Jev routed nearly everything to
simple
, even tasks requiring an LRU cache trace or modular exponentiation. TypeSafe's documentation warns against this exact anti-pattern. If a question weighs multiple factors or requires a meta-judgment, decompose it into an atomic check.
When we replaced the broad Choice question with one atomic Noul question, it fixed the separation immediately. The question was: does answering this require performing more than one sequential calculation, simulation step or logical deduction, rather than a single direct lookup, format check or one-step classification?
def call_jev(question_text):
body = {
"state": question_text,
"model": "jev-latest",
"questions": {
"multi_step": {
"type": "noul",
"instructions": (
"Answering this requires performing more than one "
"sequential calculation, simulation step, or logical "
"deduction, rather than a single direct lookup, format "
"check, or one-step classification."
),
}
},
}
# Send the request above to the classifier's API.
# response.answers["multi_step"].noul is the probability used to route.
Python
Copied
On those initial 16 tasks, Jev routed 13 of 16 in agreement with our hand-labeled difficulty on the first run and 14 of 16 on the second pass. Many engineering teams ask whether they even need a classifier API when they can write a zero-cost regex and prompt-length heuristic in Python, matching words like
sequence
,
modulo
and
race condition
or escalating any prompt over 35 words.
On the 16 development questions used to write those exact rules, the local heuristic scored 15 of 16, or 93.8%. To test whether that heuristic survived contact with realistic coding-agent traffic, we froze its code without changing a character and added 34 unseen held-out tasks across seven coding-agent buckets: fact extraction, schema validation, short classification, single-hop code checks, state simulation traces, math or logic chains and subtle language-semantics bugs.
On the 34 held-out questions, the frozen heuristic dropped 23.2 percentage points to 70.6%. Realistic simple tasks such as extracting a port from a Kubernetes YAML manifest, a file path from a unified git diff header or a line number from a Python traceback exceeded 35 words and triggered false escalations. Conversely, concise multi-step code traces such as mutable default arguments across calls, Python dictionary key hashing on
{1: "a", True: "b", 1.0: "c"}
and C short-circuit evaluation lacked the heuristic's hardcoded puzzle words and were falsely routed to the simple path. Jev classified all 34 unseen tasks with 100.0% agreement, 34 of 34, reaching 48 of 50, or 96.0%, across the full suite.
2. MaxOutputTokens is a ceiling, not a thinking-budget dial
A common mistake when building a fast-path router is assuming that setting a low maxOutputTokens cap on a reasoning model will make it spend less on easy tasks. Our 50-question data shows why that assumption fails.
When we compared
gemini-3.8-flash
with
maxOutputTokens=300
against
gemini-3.8-flash
with
maxOutputTokens=4096
while leaving
thinkingConfig
at the API default, both configurations spent almost identical thinking tokens on the 27 tasks Jev labeled
SIMPLE
:
Note:
Figures reflect single-run experimental measurements on a sample test suite; actual latencies, token counts, and billed costs will vary based on prompt length, context caching, and production load.
Capping the model's output at 300 tokens didn't save any money on easy tasks. The cap is only a ceiling, and easy answers never came close to it. On the easy tasks, the capped version actually cost slightly more than the uncapped one. All the cap did was break 7 of the 25 hard tasks. On six of them, the model ran out of room while still reasoning and never gave an answer. On the seventh, it squeezed its reasoning to fit, finished on time and got the answer wrong.
So a Jev router that sends easy tasks to the capped model and hard ones to normal Flash got all 50 right. It still cost slightly more than skipping the router and using normal Flash for everything, and it was slower. If your cheap option doesn't actually make the model think less on easy tasks, no router can save you money. Not even a perfect one that costs nothing.
3. Benchmark Jev against the strongest setup without a router
The obvious way to spend less on thinking is to ask the model to think less. So we ran a second round of tests with two lighter options: Flash-Lite, which doesn't think at all by default, and Gemini 3.8 Flash with its thinking level set to low. We added those results to the same results file, matched question by question.
A note on timing. Most of the router's time per task is spent in Flash-Lite and Flash calls, which we measured in the same run and time window as the plain Flash baseline, so the speed comparison between them is fair. Jev's own decision is a small share of the total and comes from the first round. Speed comparisons against default Flash or Pro mix the two rounds, so read those as approximate.
Note
: Figures reflect single-run experimental measurements on a sample test suite; actual latencies, token counts, and billed costs will vary based on prompt length, context caching, and production load.
The 7-bucket breakdown shows where
gemini-3.5-flash-lite
and the heuristic router missed tasks and how
Router Jev: Flash-Lite to 3.8 LOW
recovered 100% accuracy:
The strongest setup without a router was Gemini 3.8 Flash on low thinking. It solved all 50 tasks. That's the number a router had to beat.
The Jev router beat it.
It sends every task to Flash-Lite first and escalates only what Jev flags as complex. It also solved all 50 tasks, and it can help reduce both cost and response time compared with running low thinking on everything. On prompts this short the cost difference per task is small, so for an interactive agent the shorter wait is the bigger benefit.
Why it works.
On its own, Flash-Lite answered every simple task in half a second but missed 6 of the 25 hard ones. Jev flagged all 6 as complex with high confidence and escalated them. That brought its cost close to what a perfect router would achieve.
The keyword heuristic was cheaper
, but only because it got things wrong. It sent 5 hard tasks to Flash-Lite, and 2 of them failed, for 48 of 50.
Escalating to a heavier setting didn't pay here
. Routing hard tasks to Flash on default thinking was cheaper than running default thinking everywhere. It still cost more than running low thinking on everything, which already solved all 50. A heavier escalation target only makes sense when the low setting starts failing.
Limits: one run per setup, 50 prompts with hand-assigned difficulty and simple automatic grading.
4. Price per token doesn't tell the whole story
Two things in our results only show up once you look past it.
Routing and caching pull in opposite directions.
Our test prompts were short, standalone tasks, and on those the Jev router helped reduce both cost and response time. Real coding agents often look different. They send the same big block of context on every turn, such as a map of the repository and the tool definitions. Agent Platform Context Caching stores that block so you pay 75% to 90% less to resend it. The catch is that a cache belongs to one model. If your agent switches between Flash-Lite and Flash from turn to turn, it either keeps two caches or loses the discount. The practical split: route short, self-contained tasks like log parsing or schema checks, and keep long, context-heavy turns on one model.
Match the model to the workload.
Gemini 3.1 Pro is built for deep, multi-step reasoning, and it brings that same depth to every request, including short lookups that don't need it. For a workload made mostly of quick checks and extractions, a Flash configuration is the better fit, and Pro is best saved for the tasks that need its reasoning depth. Model configurations can also apply different safety settings to security-related prompts. In our run, the Pro configuration declined two short code-security review prompts that Flash answered. If your agent performs security reviews, test those prompts on the configuration you plan to use.
Cost per successful task needs the right denominator
Other ways to build the router.
Jev is one way to get a fast classifier, but not the only one. The
Getting started with discriminative models
codelab runs the same Choice, Score and Noul questions on DiffusionGemma, Google DeepMind's open-weights model, hosted on a Compute Engine GPU VM or on Cloud Run in your own Google Cloud project. An open-source server exposes the same API in front of it, so the routing code in this article only needs a different endpoint. Our results come from Jev, so measure accuracy and latency on your own tasks before switching, and keep in mind that a self-hosted model is billed by the GPU-hour rather than by the token.
Taken together, the results give three practical rules.
Start with Flash on low thinking before you build a router.
It solved all 50 tasks and cost considerably less than the default setting. Lowering the output token limit is not a substitute, because it doesn't reduce how much the model thinks on easy tasks. Set the thinking level directly, with thinkingLevel: "LOW".
Use Jev to route short, standalone tasks.
Send simple tasks to Flash-Lite and hard ones to Flash on low thinking. Ask Jev one simple yes-or-no question per factor. In our test, this helped reduce cost and response time compared with running Flash on low thinking for everything, and came close to what a perfect router would achieve. Keep long, context-heavy turns on a single model so caching keeps working. For high-volume warehouse workloads,
Jeff Nelson's BigQuery and Cloud Run cascade pattern
applies the same idea.
Measure what your agent actually spends.
Send your agent's traces and thinking-token counts to Cloud Logging and BigQuery, so you can see which tasks drive your spend and catch truncation or retries that inflate it. The benchmark code will be published after open-source review.
In summary, the most cost-effective way to run an agent is to match each task to the model that fits it.
Start with a fast model on a light setting. You'll often find it already gets the job done. Then add a small, almost free classifier like Jev to send only the hard tasks to a stronger model, and ask simple yes-or-no questions rather than one broad one. Judge every option by what it costs per task done right, not per token.

Summary
Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk) enhances enterprise AI with advanced coding, cybersecurity, and document reasoning, while Mistral Studio provides a flexible platform for deploying agents, workflows, and apps across cloud, VPC, or on-premises environments. New features like managed agents, workflows, and enterprise context streamline business processes, enabling faster development and deployment of AI solutions. Customers like ABANCA and BNP Paribas already use Studio to automate tasks, improve efficiency, and maintain full control over their AI systems.
Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk) pushes the frontier of what enterprises can build with open models. It does great for
coding
, delivers advanced
defensive cybersecurity capabilities
, and brings powerful reasoning to
complex documents
and
business tasks
.
Mistral Studio is our enterprise AI platform for putting that intelligence to work in your business. It lets your teams activate models quickly through agents, workflows and apps connected to your enterprise data and systems. Deploy them wherever you choose: in the cloud, in your own VPC, on-premises or across a combination of environments. And retain full control and understanding of the intelligence you create, from how your systems work to the knowledge they build.
Today, we’re expanding Studio with managed agents and apps, alongside new capabilities for workflows, enterprise context, agent observability and evaluations.
Customers and partners including ABANCA, Accenture, Alten, BNP Paribas, Capgemini, CMA CGM and Tata Consultancy Services already use Studio in production. With this release, your developers can build and deploy new use cases faster, then reuse that work across more of the business.
Mistral Studio is our platform for building enterprise AI applications. Running it in our own cloud environment, with inference provided by Mistral, allows us to bring AI into the business while retaining control over our infrastructure and how sensitive customer data is accessed and used.
Jose Jorge Garcia Romaris, Head of Data Engineering & AI
Our clients are looking beyond isolated AI use cases to reinvent how work gets done across the enterprise. Mistral Studio gives us the foundation to build, orchestrate and scale AI solutions tailored to their business needs, while securing control over their data and deployment. Combined with our industry expertise and delivery capabilities, it allows us to turn technology into real business impact at scale.
Gregory Christophe, Accenture x Mistral Business Group
Most industrial AI projects still stall at the pilot stage. We'll build agents and workflows for our clients' engineering and R&D teams on Mistral Studio to take their pilots into production. We're training our developers on the platform.
Gualtiero Bazzana, ExCom Member and CAIO
The AI systems we build run some of our most sensitive processes, so we run Mistral Studio on our own infrastructure and keep those systems under our control.
Su YANG - Head of Artificial Intelligence & IT Innovation, BNP Paribas
AI creates lasting value only when enterprises can trust it within their operations. Mistral Studio aims to let us decide exactly which systems the agents can access, and brings the observability and evaluation needed to turn a promising PoC into a system they can operate, measure, and rely on. That’s one of the gaps our clients are looking to close leveraging Mistral.
Fernando Alvarez, Capgemini Group Chief Strategy & Development Officer, Group Executive Board Member
We've built AI systems with Mistral's engineers for some of our most critical processes, from cargo release and customer assistance in shipping to transport orders in logistics. They run on Mistral Studio, where each new process we automate is production-ready in weeks rather than months. With the new version of Studio, our own teams and partners will do more of the building themselves, so we can take more of our processes to production and keep the know-how in-house.
Julien Smadja, VP AI
The future of enterprise AI will be defined by an ecosystem that balances innovation with trust, giving organizations the flexibility to adopt the right AI technologies while maintaining control. Through our partnership with Mistral, TCS is helping enterprises harness advanced AI capabilities while maintaining sovereignty, governance, security, and deployment flexibility. As one of the first global systems integrators investing in the Mistral ecosystem, we are enabling clients to build, deploy, govern, and scale AI with confidence. Together, we are accelerating the adoption of trusted AI and helping enterprises convert AI ambition into business outcomes.
Amit Kapur, Chief AI & Services Transformation Officer
Agents, workflows and apps for your business processes
Agents, workflows and apps serve different parts of a business process. An agent investigates and acts, a workflow coordinates execution and approvals, and an app gives employees a way to use these systems.
Studio brings all three together on shared infrastructure. You start with a model like Le Chonk and connect it to your enterprise data and systems through connectors and MCP servers. That foundation lets you easily build agents, workflows and apps with access to the context they need. Studio manages how they run and lets teams inspect what happened.
Through the new Mistral MCP server, developers can build with Mistral Vibe or the coding agent they already use, test locally and deploy to their Studio environment with one command. Studio handles hosting and execution, so teams can build on that foundation to get each new use case into production faster.
Build managed agents that investigate and act
In Studio, developers can now build agents that carry out complex, multi-step tasks. Developers can equip them with skills that capture the team’s procedures, sandboxes where they can run code, and subagents to delegate parts of a task. Hooks let developers add custom logic at key points in execution, shaping how the agent works and integrates with existing systems.
Studio manages the runtime behind all that work, using the proven infrastructure that supports millions of Mistral Vibe sessions each week. Developers can focus on the agent’s capabilities and behaviour, while setting boundaries on the tools, data and actions it can access. That means getting capable agents into production faster, with less infrastructure to build and more control over how
your agents operate.
Our engineering team built an agent in Studio to investigate production incidents. When an alert fires, engineers need to work out what happened, often under pressure to resolve the issue. The agent starts the investigation: it follows the team’s runbook, asks for approval before taking sensitive actions and posts its findings in Slack. Engineers pick up the investigation with useful context already gathered, saving the team hundreds of hours each month.
Automate processes with workflows
Workflows define how a process runs: which steps follow fixed rules, where an agent reasons and when a person decides. Interrupted runs can resume where they left off. Teams can describe a process in Mistral Vibe and use it to generate, test and deploy a workflow, with code they can inspect and edit. Today’s release also adds event triggers from enterprise systems and a visual graph that makes each workflow’s logic easier to inspect.
Our product operations team built a workflow in Studio to sort ideas from internal teams and feedback from customers. Routing each submission to the right people is one of the team’s routine tasks, but one that takes time. A model identifies bugs and feature requests, then routing rules send them to the appropriate team. This saves the product operations team about 35 hours a week.
Build apps ready for enterprise use
Coding agents make it easy to build an application, but putting it to work across an enterprise means meeting requirements for security, access and reliability. Studio provides hosting, authentication and access controls, helping developers get applications ready for enterprise use faster. Teams can build with pre-approved, reusable components, reducing the amount of new code that needs security review.
These applications can use agents and workflows, retrieve enterprise documents through search indexes and access shared context in Studio. Developers can test locally, then deploy with one command to make the application available at its own link or inside Mistral Vibe.
Our Applied AI team, which helps customers build AI solutions, built a staffing app in Studio. Previously, staffing a project meant manually matching team profiles and past experience against requirements spread across documents and tools.
The app uses an agent to recommend people and explain how their experience fits the project. Staffing leads get a shortlist with supporting evidence ready to review, helping Mistral assemble teams faster and uncover expertise that might otherwise be overlooked when staffing complex customer AI projects.
Each use case leaves the enterprise better equipped to build the next. More engineering effort goes into improving operations, with less time spent rebuilding the infrastructure around them.
Keep your AI sovereign
Studio gives you control over where your AI runs, how it operates and the intelligence you build. Deploy both the models and the platform in your own cloud, VPC or on-premises environment. You can also use Mistral-hosted deployments or combine environments to meet your requirements. Sensitive data and the processes built around it can stay within your perimeter.
You choose the models, govern access to data and tools, and decide which actions require human approval. OpenTelemetry traces show each step of a run, including model calls, tool use and approvals, so your teams can see where a process slows down or fails. Evaluations let them test changes to prompts, models or tools against your own datasets before release. Those traces and evaluations remain theirs, preserving the operational knowledge they build through use.
Customers are already putting this into practice with systems built alongside our Solutions team. From penetration testing to KYC onboarding, they’re bringing
AI into critical operations
while keeping sensitive data and specialist knowledge under their control.

Summary
Mistral released Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal model, now available with improved coding, cybersecurity, and reasoning efficiency. It leads open-weight benchmarks in coding and defensive security while offering three reasoning modes for cost-performance balance. Fully open-weight and European-trained, it empowers sovereign AI with customizable, self-hosted deployment options.
We release the weights of Le Chonk, advancing the frontier of open models in agentic coding and cybersecurity.
Earlier this month, we released Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), our flagship 1-trillion-parameter, natively multimodal model, in public preview. The response to the preview has exceeded our expectations, and we're grateful to our developer community, early-access customers, and partners for their support, collaboration, and feedback.
Since then, we've put that feedback to work while continuing to scale reinforcement learning, driving massive improvements in
coding
and defensive
cybersecurity
. Gains continue to accelerate, with no signs of saturation.
Today, we're releasing the weights of this improved Mistral Large 4.
The new model also features substantial gains in reasoning efficiency that give developers greater performance while lowering inference costs.
Mistral Large 4 ranks as the
best open-weight model for coding
and among the world's most capable open models overall. Trained from scratch on European infrastructure with clear lineage from inception to release, it gives organizations a trusted foundation for Sovereign AI
Mistral is defining the sovereign AI category and leading the open frontier. We're committed to building the world's most capable models and releasing them openly, giving developers, enterprises, and institutions the power to own, customize, and control their AI.
Built for the Builders.
Mistral Large 4 entered public preview with strong results across leading coding benchmarks. Just three weeks of additional reinforcement learning have since propelled it to the forefront of open-weight coding, taking the lead on FrontierCode and Terminal-Bench while matching the best open-weight models on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with substantially greater token efficiency.
On Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark, which assesses end-to-end code quality and whether a repository maintainer would merge the agent's change, Mistral Large 4 leads with a score of 19.7%.
Cognition - FrontierCode 2.0

Pushing the pareto frontier for agentic coding.
Mistral Large 4 delivers frontier coding performance with significantly fewer tokens, making sophisticated coding agents more economical to run at scale.
On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Mistral Large 4 scores 48%, effectively tied with the leading open-weight model, GLM-5.3, while using 47% fewer tokens per task on average.
Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index vs. Token Efficiency

The gains extend to terminal-based coding workflows. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Mistral Large 4 improved by 13 percentage points to 41% compared to its public preview, taking the lead among open-weight models while reducing output tokens by 30%.
Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index - Terminal-Bench 4.0

Beyond benchmarks, Mistral Large 4's coding capabilities are validated by human preference. In Surge Code's blind pairwise evaluations, Mistral Large 4 was preferred over leading open-weight models including GLM-5.3, Kimi K3, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, ranking behind only Claude Opus 5.5 among the models evaluated.

Built for the Defenders.
Since its preview, we've been working with leading cybersecurity vendors to evaluate Mistral Large 4 in real-world environments to test Mistral Large 4’s strengths in vulnerability reproduction and patching.
Mistral Large 4 scores 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, which measures a model’s ability to discover vulnerabilities in a codebase, reproduce and validate them, and patch them without breaking existing functionality. Crucially, Mistral Large 4 handles these legitimate defensive security tasks without unnecessary refusals.
Artificial Analysis - Cyber Index
Download PNG
Download SVG
Safety has improved alongside capability. Our model’s built-in guardrails distinguishes between defensive and malicious, offensive cybersecurity tasks. It retains strong performance on Cyber benchmarks, while achieving an average refusal rate of 96.6% on malicious cyber requests, the highest we measure among open models.
Refusal of harmful cyber requests
